quests.instruction: Choose the hidden assumption the argument depends on.
quests.prompt: 'Our sales dropped after we changed the logo, so the new logo is bad for business.'
options: The logo change, not something else, caused the drop.
Logos are important for every business.
Sales always fall in the summer months.
The old logo was popular with customers.
quests.hint: Ask what must be true for the conclusion to follow.
quests.explanation: The argument assumes the logo caused the fall in sales. Without that assumption, the timing alone proves nothing.

quests.instruction: Which assumption does the argument rely on?
quests.prompt: 'The bakery is always crowded, so it must have the best bread in town.'
options: Crowds show that its bread is better than other bakeries' bread.
The bakery is popular in other towns as well.
Crowded shops are usually noisy for customers.
Bakeries make their bread early in the morning.
quests.hint: The argument moves from 'crowded' to 'best'. What links them?
quests.explanation: The argument assumes that crowds are caused by quality. Crowds could also come from location or price.

quests.instruction: Which assumption is hidden in the argument?
quests.prompt: 'She scored highly in the interview, so she will be a great team player.'
options: Interviews are held in meeting rooms at most companies.
Interview performance predicts how well someone works with a team.
The interview was long enough to ask many questions.
Team players should be able to speak clearly.
quests.hint: What must you believe for the first statement to support the second?
quests.explanation: The conclusion is only supported if interview scores predict teamwork. The other statements are not required.

quests.instruction: Choose the assumption that connects the reason to the claim.
quests.prompt: Claim: The school should serve free breakfast. Reason: Hungry students cannot concentrate.
options: Students concentrate best in the afternoon.
Some students arrive at school without having eaten.
The school kitchen is large enough for everyone.
Breakfast is the most expensive meal of the day.
quests.hint: The reason only supports the claim if there are hungry students.
quests.explanation: The argument assumes some students really do arrive hungry. Otherwise free breakfast would not help.

quests.instruction: Which assumption links the reason to the claim?
quests.prompt: Claim: The shop should open earlier. Reason: Commuters would buy coffee on their way to work.
options: All commuters start work at exactly the same time.
Coffee is the most profitable product in the shop.
The shop already has enough staff for early hours.
Enough commuters pass the shop early and would stop to buy.
quests.hint: The reason works only if the customers exist.
quests.explanation: The argument depends on commuters actually passing and stopping. Profit, timing and staffing are separate issues.

quests.instruction: Choose the assumption the argument needs.
quests.prompt: Claim: The library should stock more graphic novels. Reason: Teenagers enjoy them.
options: Teenagers do not read anything except graphic novels.
Graphic novels cost less than most other books to buy.
More teenagers would visit and borrow if graphic novels were available.
Graphic novels are shorter than most other types of book.
quests.hint: What must happen for the reason to help the library?
quests.explanation: The claim assumes that enjoyment turns into more visits and loans. Length, exclusivity and price are not required.

quests.instruction: Which conclusion goes beyond what the data show?
quests.prompt: Data: Cities with more ice cream shops also have more sunburn cases.
options: More study would be needed to know why the pattern exists.
Ice cream shops and sunburn cases tend to appear together.
Ice cream shops cause sunburn.
Both may be linked to hot weather in those cities.
quests.hint: A pattern showing two things together does not prove one causes the other.
quests.explanation: Ice cream and sunburn both rise with hot weather. The statement that one causes the other is unsupported.

quests.instruction: Which conclusion is best supported?
quests.prompt: Data: Students who use the library often tend to get higher marks.
options: Frequent library use is linked to higher marks, though other factors may play a role.
Marks would rise for everyone if the library opened longer, because students would then have more time to study.
Going to the library causes students to get higher marks, so schools should require students to visit each week.
Students who get high marks must spend a lot of time in the library, since that is where the best students work.
quests.hint: Choose the sentence that describes the pattern without overstating it.
quests.explanation: The best sentence reports a link and admits other factors. The alternatives claim cause or predict outcomes.

quests.instruction: Which sentence confuses correlation with cause?
quests.prompt: Data: People who own dogs walk more each week.
options: Walking more may be one reason dog owners report better fitness.
People who own dogs tend to walk more each week.
Since dog owners walk more, owning a dog makes people healthier.
Dog ownership and walking often go together in this data.
quests.hint: Which sentence claims that one thing makes another happen?
quests.explanation: The right answer jumps from a pattern to a healthier result caused by ownership. The other statements stay with the pattern or suggest a possibility.

quests.instruction: Choose a plausible alternative explanation for the pattern.
quests.prompt: Data: Employees who drink a lot of coffee report more headaches.
options: Coffee is sold in cafés, shops and vending machines, and its price varies a great deal from place to place.
People with stressful jobs may both drink more coffee and get more headaches.
Headaches are painful and can affect a person's whole day, especially when they last into the evening.
Most employees work in offices with several floors, and many of them have to climb stairs during the day.
quests.hint: Look for a third factor that could explain both.
quests.explanation: Stress could lead to both coffee drinking and headaches. The other statements do not explain the pattern.

quests.instruction: Choose the best alternative explanation.
quests.prompt: Data: Children with more books at home get higher test scores.
options: Some children prefer video games to reading, so they may score lower on the reading tests at school.
Test scores are recorded by teachers at the school and are then sent to parents at the end of each term.
Families with more books may also have more time and money to support learning.
Books are printed on paper and are sold in shops, in libraries and at school book fairs.
quests.hint: Which sentence offers another factor behind the pattern?
quests.explanation: Family resources could explain both the books and the scores. The others don't offer another cause.

quests.instruction: Select the TWO possible explanations for the pattern.
quests.prompt: Data: Cafés near the university have more customers on weekdays.
options: Term time brings many extra people to the area.
Universities have libraries and lecture halls.
Students have free time between classes.
Cafés sell tea, coffee and small snacks.
quests.hint: Ask what could bring more customers on weekdays.
quests.explanation: Student breaks and extra people in term time explain weekday crowds. The other choices describe cafés or universities without explaining the pattern.

quests.instruction: Which conclusion is too broad for the evidence?
quests.prompt: Evidence: Three customers complained about the new menu.
options: Customers dislike the new menu.
Three customers complained about the new menu.
Some customers have complained about the new menu.
More feedback is needed to see how widespread the complaint is.
quests.hint: The evidence is three people. What can be said about all customers?
quests.explanation: Three complaints don't show what all customers think. The other statements stay within the evidence.

quests.instruction: Which claim does the evidence support?
quests.prompt: Evidence: I visited a city once, and my taxi driver was rude.
options: Taxi drivers in that city are rude.
People in that city are unfriendly.
That city has poor customer service.
The driver I met on my visit was rude.
quests.hint: One experience can only support a claim about that experience.
quests.explanation: The evidence covers one driver. The other claims generalise to a group, a city or a service.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to fix the hasty generalization.
quests.prompt: Original: 'I tried two online courses and they were boring, so online courses are boring.'
options: The two online courses I tried were boring, so I want to try more before deciding.
Online courses are always boring, as I have already shown.
Online courses are probably boring for most people who try them.
Two courses are enough to say that online learning fails.
quests.hint: Limit the claim to what you have actually experienced.
quests.explanation: This revision limits the claim to two courses and suggests more evidence. The remaining options still generalise.

quests.instruction: Choose the most accurate sentence.
quests.prompt: Topic: exercise and sleep.
options: Everyone finds that exercise helps them sleep better.
No one sleeps well without regular exercise.
Many people find that exercise helps them sleep better.
Exercise always helps people to sleep well.
quests.hint: Words like 'everyone', 'always' and 'no one' leave no room for exceptions.
quests.explanation: 'Many people' is accurate and leaves room for exceptions. The alternatives use absolute words that are easy to disprove.

quests.instruction: Choose the revision that removes the overgeneralization.
quests.prompt: Original: 'Teenagers never listen to advice.'
options: All teenagers refuse to take advice from adults.
Some teenagers ignore advice, especially when it feels like an order.
Teenagers hardly ever listen to advice at all.
Teenagers do not listen to advice from anyone, ever.
quests.hint: A more accurate claim limits how many people it covers and gives conditions.
quests.explanation: The correct revision limits the claim and adds a condition. The remaining options are still absolute.

quests.instruction: Which sentence claims only what the evidence supports?
quests.prompt: Evidence: In a survey of 40 staff at one company, 30 said they like flexible hours.
options: Flexible hours are the best system for every company.
Most of the staff surveyed at this company like flexible hours.
Workers everywhere like flexible hours.
Everyone prefers flexible hours to fixed ones.
quests.hint: Keep the claim as narrow as the sample.
quests.explanation: The best sentence refers to the surveyed staff at one company. The other choices apply to all workers or all companies.

quests.instruction: Which sample would give the most reliable opinions about a new bus timetable?
quests.prompt: Choose the best group to ask.
options: Friends and family of the person writing the survey.
People who chose to comment on a social media post.
Passengers at one stop during the morning rush.
Passengers chosen at random at different stops and times.
quests.hint: A good sample represents the whole group.
quests.explanation: A random mix at different places and times reflects all passengers. The others are narrow, close to the writer or self-selected.

quests.instruction: Why is this survey unreliable?
quests.prompt: A gym asked members as they left whether they enjoy exercise. Ninety-five percent said yes, so the writer concludes 'most people enjoy exercise.'
options: Ninety-five percent is too high a number to be true.
Gym members are more likely to enjoy exercise than people in general.
Members were surveyed in the evening rather than the morning.
The survey asked too few questions about exercise.
quests.hint: Who was left out of the sample?
quests.explanation: The sample consists of people who already chose to exercise. The other issues are minor or not evidence of unreliability.

quests.instruction: Which sample would give the fairest result?
quests.prompt: Claim: Students at the school like the new lunch menu.
options: A poll of teachers about what they think students prefer.
A survey of students from every year group, chosen randomly.
A vote by members of the lunch club.
A survey of students queueing in the canteen on the first day.
quests.hint: The sample should include the students the claim is about.
quests.explanation: Random selection across years represents all students. The remaining options are limited to a small group or ask the wrong people.

quests.instruction: Which conclusion goes too far?
quests.prompt: Evidence: The new app has been downloaded 5,000 times.
options: Thousands of people have tried the app.
The app has been downloaded many times.
The app is loved by its users.
Downloads show interest, but not necessarily satisfaction.
quests.hint: Downloading is not the same as liking.
quests.explanation: Downloads show people tried it, not that they love it. The other statements stay within the evidence.

quests.instruction: Which conclusion is best supported?
quests.prompt: Evidence: Sales rose 10% in the month after the new advertisement.
options: The advertisement raised sales by exactly 10%, so the company should make more advertisements like it.
Sales rose after the advertisement, though other factors might have contributed.
The advertisement is the best way to raise sales, so the company should stop trying other approaches.
Every advertisement the company makes will raise sales, so it should increase its advertising budget now.
quests.hint: Choose the sentence that describes what happened without claiming too much.
quests.explanation: The best sentence reports the timing and admits other possible causes. The rest claim exact cause or predict the future.

quests.instruction: Which sentence draws the strongest conclusion the evidence allows?
quests.prompt: Evidence: In a trial with 25 employees, those given quiet rooms finished tasks 15% faster.
options: In this trial, quiet rooms helped these employees finish tasks faster.
All companies should build quiet rooms immediately, because the trial has proved that they work.
Quiet rooms are the best way to raise productivity, and companies should try nothing else first.
Quiet rooms make every employee 15% faster, so the benefit will be the same for all staff.
quests.hint: Stay within the group and result actually measured.
quests.explanation: The best sentence is limited to the trial group. The alternatives generalise to everyone, recommend action or compare with other methods.

quests.instruction: Which evidence would best test the assumption?
quests.prompt: Argument: Later school start times will raise test scores, because students will sleep longer. Assumption: students would use the extra time to sleep.
options: The average test scores of students in other schools, taken from the most recent national report.
The number of subjects students study each week, compared with the number studied in earlier years.
The length of the school day in different countries, compared with the length of the day in ours.
A record of when students actually go to bed after the start time changes.
quests.hint: Test the assumption itself, not the conclusion.
quests.explanation: Bedtime records show whether students really sleep more. The other options don't test the assumption.

quests.instruction: Which evidence would best test the assumption?
quests.prompt: Argument: Free parking would bring more shoppers. Assumption: shoppers avoid the town centre because of parking costs.
options: The price of goods in town centre shops, compared with the prices in the out-of-town stores.
Interviews with shoppers about why they avoid the town centre.
The opening hours of the main car park, compared with the opening hours of the shops nearby.
The number of parking spaces in the town centre, counted on a typical weekday afternoon.
quests.hint: Which evidence would show the shoppers' actual reasons?
quests.explanation: Asking shoppers reveals whether parking costs really stop them. The alternatives concern spaces, goods or hours.

quests.instruction: Which evidence would best test the assumption?
quests.prompt: Argument: A smartphone app will make customers loyal. Assumption: customers will actually use the app.
options: A list of the features the app will include, such as offers, reminders and a simple loyalty card.
A pilot where a small group uses the app and their repeat visits are tracked.
Reviews of unrelated apps from other companies, collected from the online store over several years.
The cost of developing the app for the shop, including design, testing and the first year of support.
quests.hint: The test should measure real behaviour.
quests.explanation: A pilot shows whether customers use the app and return. The remaining options describe features, costs or unrelated apps.

quests.instruction: Which hidden assumption does the argument rely on?
quests.prompt: 'Most students at the school own a smartphone, so all homework should be digital.'
options: Owning a smartphone means students can complete homework on it.
Digital homework is cheaper for teachers to mark.
Smartphones have larger screens than laptops or tablets.
Most students prefer paper homework to digital homework.
quests.hint: Ask what the first statement quietly takes for granted.
quests.explanation: The argument assumes owning a phone is enough to do homework. Marking cost, paper preference and screen size are not part of the argument.

quests.instruction: Which conclusion is best supported?
quests.prompt: Evidence: Two of the ten new hires resigned within six months.
options: New hires do not like the company.
The company has a high staff turnover.
Two of these ten hires left within six months.
The hiring process was a failure.
quests.hint: Choose the conclusion that stays with the numbers given.
quests.explanation: This statement repeats what the evidence shows. The others draw wider conclusions about turnover, opinions or the process.

quests.instruction: Select the TWO problems with this reasoning.
quests.prompt: 'Our team had its best sales month after buying a coffee machine, so the coffee machine boosts sales.'
options: It talks about a team instead of a whole company.
It mentions coffee, which is unrelated to work.
It ignores other explanations, such as seasonal demand.
It assumes the machine caused the increase.
quests.hint: Focus on what the reasoning skips over.
quests.explanation: The argument assumes cause and ignores other explanations. Mentioning coffee or a team isn't the flaw.
